screens.title: BGP Path Attributes and Best Path Selection
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you will learn how BGP carries a set of path attributes that together determine which route a router selects when multiple choices exist. These attributes include local settings like WEIGHT, AS-wide preferences such as LOCAL_PREF, transitive indicators like AS_PATH and ORIGIN, and cross-AS hints such as MED and NEXT_HOP. Understanding the scope and default value of each attribute matters because some control outbound traffic inside your autonomous system, while others affect inbound choices by remote ASes. We'll also walk through the step-by-step best path selection algorithm so you can predict how a change to one attribute will or will not alter forwarding. For example, setting a higher LOCAL_PREF on routes from one ISP makes all routers in your AS prefer that exit point for outbound traffic, while changing WEIGHT on a single router affects only that device. Throughout, watch for common misconceptions: attributes have different scopes and are evaluated in strict order. By the end of this lesson you will be able to read show ip bgp output, explain why a path was chosen, and make safe, scoped attribute changes in a lab before applying them in production.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of this chapter you will identify and categorize the most common BGP path attributes such as WEIGHT, LOCAL_PREF, AS_PATH, ORIGIN, MED, and NEXT_HOP, and explain their default behavior and scope. You will also be able to describe each attribute's practical effect with a concrete example, like how setting LOCAL_PREF on routes from one ISP affects outbound routing for an entire AS. Next, you will learn the deterministic best path selection algorithm and trace how attributes are evaluated step-by-step so you can predict which path a router selects. Finally, you will analyze real show ip bgp outputs and manipulate WEIGHT or LOCAL_PREF in a lab to verify behavior. These skills matter because incorrect assumptions about scope or order can lead to ineffective policies: a LOCAL_PREF change does not influence an adjacent AS, and a WEIGHT change only affects the local router. Practice will build confidence with both troubleshooting and safe traffic-engineering changes.

screens.title: Bloom's Progression
screens.narratorSegment: We will structure learning using a Bloom-style progression: first you learn attribute names and categories, then you understand their defaults and scope, next you apply that knowledge to influence routing in a lab, and finally you master prediction of path selection across multiple routers. Start by learning: memorize attribute names and what they mean. Then understand: compare WEIGHT, LOCAL_PREF, AS_PATH and their scopes so you can reason about propagation. Apply that knowledge by changing WEIGHT or LOCAL_PREF in a lab and verifying results with show ip bgp. Mastery comes when you can look at multiple routes and explain exactly why one path wins based on the algorithm order. This progression helps avoid common mistakes like confusing LOCAL_PREF and MED or assuming a WEIGHT change will be visible across the AS. Practicing each level builds confidence to plan safe traffic-engineering changes.

screens.title: BGP Path Attribute Categories
screens.narratorSegment: BGP path attributes are grouped into four categories that determine if implementations must recognize them and whether they should be passed to other peers. The first category, well-known mandatory, includes attributes that every router must support and must include in UPDATE messages — AS_PATH, NEXT_HOP and ORIGIN are examples. Well-known discretionary attributes must be recognized by all routers but may be omitted from updates; LOCAL_PREF and ATOMIC_AGGREGATE fall here. Optional transitive attributes may not be recognized by all implementations but must be forwarded; COMMUNITY is a common example. Optional non-transitive attributes are only forwarded if recognized; MED is often treated this way. A concrete example: COMMUNITY tags are optional and transitive, so if a router doesn't understand a COMMUNITY value it still forwards it to other peers. A common misconception is assuming all optional attributes are dropped when unrecognized — transitive optional attributes are preserved. Why this matters: configuration and policy decisions depend on propagation rules. If you tag routes with a non-transitive attribute and expect others to act on it across an untrusted path, the tag may disappear. Key takeaway: choose attribute-based policies with propagation behavior in mind and test whether attributes survive forwarding in your topology.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Attribute Categories

Four categories

These categories dictate whether attributes must be recognized, must appear, and whether they get forwarded to other peers.

Well-known mandatory
Must be recognized and present; e.g., AS_PATH, NEXT_HOP, ORIGIN.
Well-known discretionary
Recognized by all but may be omitted; e.g., LOCAL_PREF.
Optional transitive
May be unrecognized but must be forwarded; e.g., COMMUNITY.
Optional non-transitive
Forwarded only if recognized; MED is commonly non-transitive.

Concrete example

If Router A tags a route with a COMMUNITY and an intermediate router doesn’t understand that COMMUNITY, the intermediate device still forwards the COMMUNITY onward. If Router A uses a non-transitive tag that an intermediate doesn’t understand, the tag may be removed.

Key Takeaway

Attribute propagation differs by category. Pick attributes with the correct propagation behavior for your policy goals.

screens.title: WEIGHT — A Local Preference on the Router
screens.narratorSegment: The WEIGHT attribute is a Cisco-proprietary value that exists only on the local router and is the very first attribute evaluated by the best path algorithm. A route with a higher WEIGHT wins immediately without considering any other attributes. The default WEIGHT is 32768 for routes locally originated on the router and 0 for routes learned from peers. A practical example: on R1 you might set neighbor 192.168.12.2 weight 500 so R1 prefers the path learned from that neighbor for outbound traffic, even if other routers in the AS prefer a different exit. Because WEIGHT is local, a common misconception is thinking changing it on one router will alter the AS-wide path — it will not. That means WEIGHT is powerful for per-router traffic decisions but not appropriate for AS-wide policy. Use WEIGHT when you want to alter only the local router's selection, such as controlling which uplink that router itself uses for specific prefixes. Always test changes in a lab and verify with show ip bgp and show ip route: WEIGHT changes will appear only on the device you configured.

keyIdea.title: WEIGHT Summary
keyIdea.text: WEIGHT is local to a router and wins before any other attribute; use it for per-router preferences and lab testing.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › WEIGHT

WEIGHT basics

A Cisco-only attribute, checked first in the algorithm. Higher value preferred. Default: 32768 for local, 0 for learned.

Use case
Prefer a single router's uplink for certain prefixes without changing the AS-wide policy.
Common mistake

Expecting WEIGHT to propagate across the AS. It does not — it affects only the configured router.

Concrete example

On R1 set neighbor 192.168.12.2 weight 500 to prefer routes from that neighbor for R1's outbound traffic. Other routers won't change their selection.

! On R1
router bgp 65001
 neighbor 192.168.12.2 remote-as 65002
 neighbor 192.168.12.2 weight 500

! Verify
show ip bgp 2.2.2.0
Key Takeaway

WEIGHT overrides all other attributes on a router. Use it selectively for per-router control.

screens.title: LOCAL_PREF — AS-wide Exit Preference
screens.narratorSegment: LOCAL_PREF, or Local Preference, is an attribute exchanged only among iBGP peers within the same autonomous system. It indicates which exit point routers inside the AS should use to reach a destination. A higher LOCAL_PREF is preferred and the default is 100. For example, if your AS connects to ISP-A and ISP-B and you want most outbound traffic to leave via ISP-A, set LOCAL_PREF higher on routes learned from ISP-A; every router in the AS that sees that LOCAL_PREF will prefer ISP-A as the exit. Importantly, LOCAL_PREF is not sent to eBGP peers, so it cannot directly influence an adjacent AS’s inbound choice — using LOCAL_PREF to try to affect an external AS is a common pitfall. Instead, MED or other inter-AS mechanisms are used for influencing inbound traffic. Another practical note: since LOCAL_PREF is evaluated immediately after WEIGHT in the algorithm, it can decisively override differences in AS_PATH or MED. Use route-maps or inbound policy at your AS edge to set LOCAL_PREF consistently for predictable outbound behavior, and always validate across multiple routers to ensure propagation via iBGP is functioning as expected.

keyIdea.title: LOCAL_PREF Summary
keyIdea.text: LOCAL_PREF is AS-wide and determines how routers inside your AS prefer exit points; higher is better and default is 100.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › LOCAL_PREF

What LOCAL_PREF is

An attribute used within an AS to indicate preferred exit points. Higher values are preferred; default 100.

Use case
Prefer ISP-A as AS exit by assigning higher LOCAL_PREF to routes from ISP-A.
Common pitfall

Trying to use LOCAL_PREF to influence another AS’s inbound routing. LOCAL_PREF is not advertised to eBGP peers.

Concrete scenario

AS 65000 peers with ISP-A and ISP-B. To make ISP-A preferred for outbound, set LOCAL_PREF 200 for routes received from ISP-A and leave ISP-B at 100. All routers in AS 65000 will then prefer ISP-A when choosing outbound paths.

Key Takeaway

LOCAL_PREF controls AS-wide outbound selection. Use it when you need consistent exit-point behavior across your AS.

screens.title: AS_PATH and Loop Prevention
screens.narratorSegment: AS_PATH is a fundamental, well-known, mandatory attribute listing the autonomous systems a route has traversed. It is ordered from the nearest AS to the origin AS and is crucial for both preference and loop prevention. In practical terms, BGP prefers shorter AS_PATHs because fewer AS hops usually imply a closer or more direct route. For example, if a route arrives with AS_PATH 65002 65003 it has traversed those ASes to reach you; if you receive the same prefix with AS_PATH 65004, the shorter single-hop path is preferred when earlier attributes tie. AS_PATH is also used to prevent loops: if a router sees its own AS number in the AS_PATH, it rejects the route to avoid looping. A common policy technique is AS_PATH prepending, where you intentionally add your ASN multiple times to make a path appear longer and therefore less preferred by upstream ASes. Be careful with prepending: it affects how external peers rank your routes and can have unintended global impacts if overused. Always validate changes and understand that AS_PATH is transitive and visible across AS boundaries. AS_PATH and Loop Prevention means as_path shows the route's as hop sequence, helps prevent loops, and shorter paths are generally preferred.. In practical terms, a transitive list of as hops that informs preference and prevents loops. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › AS_PATH

AS_PATH mechanics

Lists ASNs a route passed through. Shorter AS_PATHs are preferred; presence of your ASN indicates a loop and the route is discarded.

Loop prevention
If your ASN appears in AS_PATH, you must reject to avoid loops.
Policy note

AS_PATH prepending lengthens the visible path to reduce preference by other ASes.

Example

Two advertisements for 10.0.0.0/24 arrive: one with AS_PATH 65002 65003 and another with 65004. If previous attributes tie, the path with the shorter AS_PATH is chosen.

AS_PATH: 65002 65003 AS_PATH: 65004 Preferred: AS_PATH 65004 (shorter)
Key Takeaway

AS_PATH both informs preference and prevents loops; use prepending deliberately and sparingly.

screens.title: ORIGIN — Where the Route Started
screens.narratorSegment: The ORIGIN attribute tells BGP how a route entered the protocol. There are three values: IGP (i), EGP (e), and Incomplete (?). IGP indicates the route was originated within BGP via the network command or came from an IGP and is the most preferred origin. EGP is a legacy code from when the Exterior Gateway Protocol existed and is rarely used today. Incomplete means the route was introduced to BGP by redistribution from another source such as an IGP or static and is the least preferred. A concrete example: a network statement that advertises 10.1.1.0 into BGP typically results in ORIGIN i. If a route is redistributed from OSPF into BGP without being originally created in BGP, it may show ORIGIN?. When comparing two otherwise equal paths, BGP prefers the lower ORIGIN type, with IGP best, then EGP, then Incomplete. A common misconception is treating ORIGIN as a long-term trust signal; it's only a simple indicator of how the route was introduced and is evaluated after AS_PATH in the selection process. Key takeaway: ORIGIN provides a simple ordering preference and helps you spot redistributed routes.

keyIdea.title: ORIGIN Summary
keyIdea.text: ORIGIN denotes the route’s source into BGP: IGP is preferred over EGP, which is preferred over Incomplete.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › ORIGIN

ORIGIN types

  • IGP (i): originated within BGP or via network command — most preferred.
  • EGP (e): legacy external protocol — rarely used.
  • Incomplete (?): learned by redistribution into BGP — least preferred.
Misconception

ORIGIN is not a security signal; it simply records how the route was introduced and affects preference order after AS_PATH.

Scenario

If a route learned from a neighbor shows ORIGIN ?, it likely came from redistribution. When AS_PATH and other attributes tie, ORIGIN will break the tie favoring IGP-originated routes.

Key Takeaway

ORIGIN ranks route-source types and helps spot redistributed prefixes during troubleshooting.

screens.title: MED — A Hint for Adjacent ASes
screens.narratorSegment: MED, or Multi-Exit Discriminator, is an attribute exchanged between eBGP peers to influence how an adjacent autonomous system selects among multiple entry points into your AS. A lower MED value is preferred. Think of MED as a polite hint to neighbors: if you have two connections into AS 65000 and you prefer inbound traffic to enter via one of them, advertise a lower MED on routes at that connection. For example, set MED 10 on routes received at the preferred entry and MED 100 on the other. Important nuances: MED is only a suggestion to the adjacent AS and many operators ignore it in favor of LOCAL_PREF or policy. MED defaults to 0 if not set. Also MED is often non-transitive, so it may not be forwarded unchanged across multiple ASes. A common mistake is relying on MED to change outbound routing for your own AS; it won't. Use MED for influencing an adjacent AS's inbound decisions, and pair it with clear peering agreements and testing. Always verify how the peer treats MED in your interconnection and avoid assuming universal compliance.

keyIdea.title: MED Summary
keyIdea.text: MED is an inter-AS hint; lower is preferred, but it is only a suggestion to the adjacent AS and may be non-transitive.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › MED

MED explained

A hint exchanged with eBGP peers to influence how they send traffic to your AS. Lower MED is preferred; default 0.

Use case
Influence inbound traffic from an adjacent AS when you have multiple interconnects.
Common misconception

Assuming MED will always be honored by the neighbor. Peers may prefer LOCAL_PREF or filter MED.

Scenario

You have two peering links to AS 65002. Advertise MED 10 on the preferred link and MED 100 on the other. The neighbor may choose the lower MED, but confirm peer behavior.

Key Takeaway

Use MED to signal preferred entry points to neighbors, but always validate peer handling and plan fallbacks.

screens.title: NEXT_HOP and IGP Reachability
screens.narratorSegment: NEXT_HOP identifies the IP address of the router that should be used to reach an advertised prefix. For eBGP the next-hop is typically the directly connected neighbor; for iBGP the next-hop learned from an eBGP peer is often carried unchanged. That means your iBGP peers must have IGP reachability to that NEXT_HOP, otherwise the route will be unusable even if it looks attractive in BGP attributes. A classic example: Router R2 advertises 2.2.2.0/24 to R1 over eBGP and sets NEXT_HOP 192.0.2.2. R1 learns the route via iBGP and retains NEXT_HOP 192.0.2.2; if other iBGP routers do not have an IGP path to 192.0.2.2 they cannot install the route. A common mistake is assuming BGP alone provides forwarding reachability — BGP selects based on attributes but IGP must supply next-hop reachability. To mitigate this, networks often use next-hop-self on eBGP sessions to set the next-hop to the advertising router, or ensure the IGP advertises reachability to external next-hops. Key takeaway: NEXT_HOP is essential for forwarding and its reachability is evaluated as part of the best path algorithm. NEXT_HOP and IGP Reachability means next_hop must be reachable via igp for a bgp-selected route to be usable; lack of reachability makes routes invalid.. In practical terms, why bgp needs igp reachability to the next hop. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

For eBGP the next-hop is typically the directly connected neighbor; for iBGP the next-hop learned from an eBGP peer is often carried unchanged. That means your iBGP peers must have IGP reachability to that NEXT_HOP, otherwise the route will be unusable even if it looks attractive in BGP attributes. A classic example: Router R2 advertises 2.2.2.0/24 to R1 over eBGP and sets NEXT_HOP 192.0.2.2. R1 learns the route via iBGP and retains NEXT_HOP 192.0.2.2; if other iBGP routers do not have an IGP path to 192.0.2.2 they cannot install the route. A common mistake is assuming BGP alone provides forwarding reachability — BGP selects based on attributes but IGP must supply next-hop reachability. To mitigate this, networks often use next-hop-self on eBGP sessions to set the next-hop to the advertising router, or ensure the IGP advertises reachability to external next-hops. Key takeaway: NEXT_HOP is essential for forwarding and its reachability is evaluated as part of the best path algorithm. NEXT_HOP and IGP Reachability means next_hop must be reachable via igp for a bgp-selected route to be usable; lack of reachability makes routes invalid.. In practical terms, why bgp needs igp reachability to the next hop. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: NEXT_HOP Summary
keyIdea.text: NEXT_HOP must be reachable via IGP for a BGP-selected route to be usable; lack of reachability makes routes invalid.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › NEXT_HOP

NEXT_HOP role

Specifies the IP address to use to forward packets toward the prefix. Reachability is required for routes to be installed.

Practical tip
Use next-hop-self or ensure IGP advertises reachability to external next-hops.
Common pitfall

Assuming a selected BGP path is usable when the NEXT_HOP is unreachable via IGP. It will be invalid.

Annotated example

R2 advertises 2.2.2.0/24 with NEXT_HOP 192.0.2.2. R1 learns via eBGP; R3 learns via iBGP from R1 and still sees NEXT_HOP 192.0.2.2. If R3’s IGP has no route to 192.0.2.2, R3 cannot use the BGP route.
Key Takeaway

BGP depends on IGP for next-hop reachability; ensure IGP coverage or normalize next-hops at eBGP boundaries.

screens.title: Best Path Algorithm — Steps 1 to 4
screens.narratorSegment: When a BGP router has multiple paths to the same prefix, it evaluates attributes in a strict order. The first four steps determine many real-world outcomes. Step 1 prefers the highest WEIGHT — a Cisco-only, local attribute that immediately wins when different. Step 2 prefers the highest LOCAL_PREF, an AS-wide setting that overrides AS_PATH and MED decisions when set differently. If WEIGHT and LOCAL_PREF tie, Step 3 prefers paths locally originated by the router, such as those installed with the network command or via redistribution. Step 4 prefers the shortest AS_PATH, so fewer AS hops are generally better. Concrete example: suppose two routes arrive — one learned from ISP-A with LOCAL_PREF 100 and AS_PATH length 2, and another learned from ISP-B with LOCAL_PREF 200 but longer AS_PATH. At step 2 the route with LOCAL_PREF 200 wins and the algorithm stops; AS_PATH is not even considered. A common misconception is thinking AS_PATH always decides the winner — LOCAL_PREF and WEIGHT are checked earlier. Closing question: given a tie in WEIGHT and LOCAL_PREF, did you check if any route is locally originated before comparing AS_PATH? That step often resolves ties in operational networks.

keyIdea.title: First Four Steps
keyIdea.text: WEIGHT → LOCAL_PREF → locally originated → AS_PATH. Higher weight/local_pref and locally originated routes take precedence before AS_PATH is considered.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Best Path: Steps 1–4

Ordered steps

1. Highest WEIGHT
Cisco local-only preference. Higher wins.
2. Highest LOCAL_PREF
AS-wide outbound preference. Higher wins.
3. Locally originated
Routes injected by this router via network or redistribution are preferred.
4. Shortest AS_PATH
Fewer AS hops is preferred when previous checks tie.

Example walk-through

Two routes: Route A LOCAL_PREF 100, AS_PATH length 2. Route B LOCAL_PREF 200, AS_PATH length 5. At step 1 WEIGHT ties; at step 2 Route B wins because of higher LOCAL_PREF and the algorithm stops — AS_PATH is not evaluated.

Key Takeaway

The algorithm is hierarchical. A higher LOCAL_PREF beats shorter AS_PATHs; know the order to predict outcomes.

screens.title: Best Path Algorithm — Steps 5 to 8
screens.narratorSegment: Continuing the best path sequence, Step 5 prefers the lowest ORIGIN type (IGP over EGP over Incomplete). If ORIGIN ties, Step 6 prefers the lowest MED, which influences inbound selection by adjacent ASes. Step 7 prefers eBGP paths over iBGP paths when all previous attributes are equal — this usually favors paths learned from external peers. Step 8 prefers the path with the lowest IGP cost to the BGP NEXT_HOP; this is a practical step because the selected BGP path must be reachable for forwarding. For example, if two paths have the same WEIGHT, LOCAL_PREF, origin and MED, but one path's NEXT_HOP is reachable with IGP cost 10 and the other has cost 5, the algorithm will select the lower IGP cost path. A frequent operational oversight is not checking IGP reachability: a route with great BGP attributes but an unreachable NEXT_HOP will not be used. Another misconception is assuming MED applies globally; MED is an inter-AS hint often ignored by peers. Key takeaway: beyond the early attribute checks, reachability considerations and eBGP preference play a crucial role in final selection.

keyIdea.title: Middle Steps
keyIdea.text: After ORIGIN and MED, eBGP is preferred over iBGP, then the router prefers the path with the lowest IGP cost to the NEXT_HOP.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Best Path: Steps 5–8

Steps 5–8

5. Lowest ORIGIN type
IGP > EGP > Incomplete.
6. Lowest MED
Lower MED preferred; a hint for adjacent ASes.
7. Prefer eBGP over iBGP
External-learned paths are favored when previous checks tie.
8. Lowest IGP cost to NEXT_HOP
Next-hop reachability and local IGP cost matter for forwarding.

Concrete example

Two equal paths reach the same prefix with identical earlier attributes. One path's NEXT_HOP is reachable in OSPF with cost 5, the other's cost is 10. Because Step 8 looks at IGP cost, the lower cost path is selected for forwarding.

Key Takeaway

Even with ideal BGP attributes, IGP reachability to NEXT_HOP must be verified; otherwise the route cannot be used.

screens.title: Best Path Algorithm — Final Tie-Breakers
screens.narratorSegment: When all previous attributes are equal, BGP uses final tie-breakers to ensure deterministic selection. Step 9 prefers the oldest path to reduce route-flap churn when comparing multiple paths from the same eBGP peer. Step 10 prefers the path from the BGP router with the lowest Router ID as a tie-breaker. If a tie still remains, Step 11 prefers the path from the neighbor with the lowest IP address. These last checks are operational safeguards to avoid non-deterministic behavior and ensure stable forwarding without oscillation. Concrete example: if two sessions from the same AS present identical attributes, the route learned earlier will be preferred; if they were learned simultaneously, the lower Router ID or neighbor IP will decide. A misconception is thinking these are policy knobs — they are not intended for traffic engineering, but as deterministic fallbacks. Key takeaway: the algorithm always results in one chosen path. If you need to change selection earlier, adjust WEIGHT or LOCAL_PREF; relying on final tie-breakers is brittle and unlikely to survive topology changes. Best Path Algorithm — Final Tie-Breakers means oldest route, then lowest router id, and finally lowest neighbor ip ensure deterministic selection when all attributes tie.. In practical terms, oldest path, lowest router id, then neighbor ip address. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Oldest route, then lowest Router ID, and finally lowest neighbor IP ensure deterministic selection when all attributes tie.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Final Tie-Breakers

Tie-breaker order

9. Oldest path
Prefer the path that has been stable the longest to reduce flapping.
10. Lowest Router ID
Choose the path learned from the peer with the lowest router ID.
11. Lowest neighbor IP
Final deterministic tie-breaker: the neighbor with the smaller IP wins.

Operational note

These steps are safeguards, not tuning levers. If you need predictable selection, adjust earlier attributes like WEIGHT or LOCAL_PREF. Using tie-breakers to engineer traffic is brittle and susceptible to topology changes.

Check your understanding

If two routes are identical in all attributes but came from different neighbors, which final tie-breaker decides the winner? Consider age, router ID, and neighbor IP in sequence.

screens.title: Lab Walkthrough — show ip bgp and Changing WEIGHT
screens.narratorSegment: This hands-on walkthrough shows how to inspect BGP attributes and safely change WEIGHT on a single router. First, establish eBGP peering between two routers, R1 in AS 65001 and R2 in AS 65002, and ensure R2 advertises a loopback network into BGP. On R1 run show ip bgp 2.2.2.0 to see the advertised route's attributes: network, next-hop, AS_PATH, origin code, MED, LOCAL_PREF, and WEIGHT. Initially a learned route will show WEIGHT 0 on R1. To prefer that path on R1 only, configure neighbor 192.168.12.2 weight 500 under R1's BGP configuration and re-run show ip bgp 2.2.2.0. You will see WEIGHT updated to 500 on R1 but unchanged on other routers. A key verification step is to check the routing table with show ip route to confirm the forwarding decision changed. Common mistakes include changing attributes on production routers without lab validation and neglecting to verify next-hop reachability. Concrete commands are shown in the visual panel; practice these steps in a simulator to see how the local WEIGHT change immediately affects only the configured router. keyIdea.text: Use show ip bgp to inspect attributes, change WEIGHT locally, and verify with show ip route that forwarding follows the selection.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Lab Walkthrough

Starter configuration

! On R2
interface Loopback0
 ip address 2.2.2.2 255.255.255.0
router bgp 65002
 neighbor 192.168.12.1 remote-as 65001
 network 2.2.2.0 mask 255.255.255.0

! On R1
router bgp 65001
 neighbor 192.168.12.2 remote-as 65002

! Verify on R1
show ip bgp 2.2.2.0
Initial output will show WEIGHT 0 for learned routes. To change WEIGHT on R1, apply the neighbor weight command and re-run the show command.

Change WEIGHT and verify

! On R1
router bgp 65001
 neighbor 192.168.12.2 weight 500

! Re-verify
show ip bgp 2.2.2.0
show ip route 2.2.2.0
Key Takeaway

WEIGHT changes only affect the router where configured. Always verify both BGP and IP routing tables to confirm forwarding follows your change.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.narratorSegment: Let's summarize the essentials you should keep in mind. First, attributes carry the policy and context that BGP uses to pick a single best route; they are grouped by propagation rules and recognition. Second, scope matters: WEIGHT is local to a router, LOCAL_PREF is AS-wide, AS_PATH and ORIGIN are transitive and visible across AS boundaries, MED is a hint to adjacent ASes, and NEXT_HOP must be reachable via IGP for forwarding. Third, the best path algorithm evaluates attributes in a strict order — WEIGHT, LOCAL_PREF, local origination, AS_PATH, ORIGIN, MED, eBGP over iBGP, IGP cost to NEXT_HOP, and final tie-breakers like age and Router ID. Finally, always validate changes in a lab environment and check both BGP and IP routing tables after modifying attributes. These points will help you design predictable traffic-engineering policies and avoid common pitfalls like assuming WEIGHT propagates or expecting MED to always be honored.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you will learn how BGP carries a set of path attributes that together determine which route a router selects when multiple choices exist. These attributes include local settings like WEIGHT, AS-wide preferences such as LOCAL_PREF, transitive indicators like AS_PATH and ORIGIN, and cross-AS hints such as MED and NEXT_HOP. Understanding the scope and default value of each attribute matters because some control outbound traffic inside your autonomous system, while others affect inbound choices by remote ASes. We'll also walk through the step-by-step best path selection algorithm so you can predict how a change to one attribute will or will not alter forwarding. For example, setting a higher LOCAL_PREF on routes from one ISP makes all routers in your AS prefer that exit point for outbound traffic, while changing WEIGHT on a single router affects only that device. Throughout, watch for common misconceptions: attributes have different scopes and are evaluated in strict order. By the end of this lesson you will be able to read show ip bgp output, explain why a path was chosen, and make safe, scoped attribute changes in a lab before applying them in production.

By the end of this chapter you will identify and categorize the most common BGP path attributes such as WEIGHT, LOCAL_PREF, AS_PATH, ORIGIN, MED, and NEXT_HOP, and explain their default behavior and scope. You will also be able to describe each attribute's practical effect with a concrete example, like how setting LOCAL_PREF on routes from one ISP affects outbound routing for an entire AS. Next, you will learn the deterministic best path selection algorithm and trace how attributes are evaluated step-by-step so you can predict which path a router selects. Finally, you will analyze real show ip bgp outputs and manipulate WEIGHT or LOCAL_PREF in a lab to verify behavior. These skills matter because incorrect assumptions about scope or order can lead to ineffective policies: a LOCAL_PREF change does not influence an adjacent AS, and a WEIGHT change only affects the local router. Practice will build confidence with both troubleshooting and safe traffic-engineering changes.

We will structure learning using a Bloom-style progression: first you learn attribute names and categories, then you understand their defaults and scope, next you apply that knowledge to influence routing in a lab, and finally you master prediction of path selection across multiple routers. Start by learning: memorize attribute names and what they mean. Then understand: compare WEIGHT, LOCAL_PREF, AS_PATH and their scopes so you can reason about propagation. Apply that knowledge by changing WEIGHT or LOCAL_PREF in a lab and verifying results with show ip bgp. Mastery comes when you can look at multiple routes and explain exactly why one path wins based on the algorithm order. This progression helps avoid common mistakes like confusing LOCAL_PREF and MED or assuming a WEIGHT change will be visible across the AS. Practicing each level builds confidence to plan safe traffic-engineering changes.

BGP path attributes are grouped into four categories that determine if implementations must recognize them and whether they should be passed to other peers. The first category, well-known mandatory, includes attributes that every router must support and must include in UPDATE messages — AS_PATH, NEXT_HOP and ORIGIN are examples. Well-known discretionary attributes must be recognized by all routers but may be omitted from updates; LOCAL_PREF and ATOMIC_AGGREGATE fall here. Optional transitive attributes may not be recognized by all implementations but must be forwarded; COMMUNITY is a common example. Optional non-transitive attributes are only forwarded if recognized; MED is often treated this way. A concrete example: COMMUNITY tags are optional and transitive, so if a router doesn't understand a COMMUNITY value it still forwards it to other peers. A common misconception is assuming all optional attributes are dropped when unrecognized — transitive optional attributes are preserved. Why this matters: configuration and policy decisions depend on propagation rules. If you tag routes with a non-transitive attribute and expect others to act on it across an untrusted path, the tag may disappear. Key takeaway: choose attribute-based policies with propagation behavior in mind and test whether attributes survive forwarding in your topology.

The WEIGHT attribute is a Cisco-proprietary value that exists only on the local router and is the very first attribute evaluated by the best path algorithm. A route with a higher WEIGHT wins immediately without considering any other attributes. The default WEIGHT is 32768 for routes locally originated on the router and 0 for routes learned from peers. A practical example: on R1 you might set neighbor 192.168.12.2 weight 500 so R1 prefers the path learned from that neighbor for outbound traffic, even if other routers in the AS prefer a different exit. Because WEIGHT is local, a common misconception is thinking changing it on one router will alter the AS-wide path — it will not. That means WEIGHT is powerful for per-router traffic decisions but not appropriate for AS-wide policy. Use WEIGHT when you want to alter only the local router's selection, such as controlling which uplink that router itself uses for specific prefixes. Always test changes in a lab and verify with show ip bgp and show ip route: WEIGHT changes will appear only on the device you configured.

LOCAL_PREF, or Local Preference, is an attribute exchanged only among iBGP peers within the same autonomous system. It indicates which exit point routers inside the AS should use to reach a destination. A higher LOCAL_PREF is preferred and the default is 100. For example, if your AS connects to ISP-A and ISP-B and you want most outbound traffic to leave via ISP-A, set LOCAL_PREF higher on routes learned from ISP-A; every router in the AS that sees that LOCAL_PREF will prefer ISP-A as the exit. Importantly, LOCAL_PREF is not sent to eBGP peers, so it cannot directly influence an adjacent AS’s inbound choice — using LOCAL_PREF to try to affect an external AS is a common pitfall. Instead, MED or other inter-AS mechanisms are used for influencing inbound traffic. Another practical note: since LOCAL_PREF is evaluated immediately after WEIGHT in the algorithm, it can decisively override differences in AS_PATH or MED. Use route-maps or inbound policy at your AS edge to set LOCAL_PREF consistently for predictable outbound behavior, and always validate across multiple routers to ensure propagation via iBGP is functioning as expected.

AS_PATH is a fundamental, well-known, mandatory attribute listing the autonomous systems a route has traversed. It is ordered from the nearest AS to the origin AS and is crucial for both preference and loop prevention. In practical terms, BGP prefers shorter AS_PATHs because fewer AS hops usually imply a closer or more direct route. For example, if a route arrives with AS_PATH 65002 65003 it has traversed those ASes to reach you; if you receive the same prefix with AS_PATH 65004, the shorter single-hop path is preferred when earlier attributes tie. AS_PATH is also used to prevent loops: if a router sees its own AS number in the AS_PATH, it rejects the route to avoid looping. A common policy technique is AS_PATH prepending, where you intentionally add your ASN multiple times to make a path appear longer and therefore less preferred by upstream ASes. Be careful with prepending: it affects how external peers rank your routes and can have unintended global impacts if overused. Always validate changes and understand that AS_PATH is transitive and visible across AS boundaries. AS_PATH and Loop Prevention means as_path shows the route's as hop sequence, helps prevent loops, and shorter paths are generally preferred.. In practical terms, a transitive list of as hops that informs preference and prevents loops. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

The ORIGIN attribute tells BGP how a route entered the protocol. There are three values: IGP (i), EGP (e), and Incomplete (?). IGP indicates the route was originated within BGP via the network command or came from an IGP and is the most preferred origin. EGP is a legacy code from when the Exterior Gateway Protocol existed and is rarely used today. Incomplete means the route was introduced to BGP by redistribution from another source such as an IGP or static and is the least preferred. A concrete example: a network statement that advertises 10.1.1.0 into BGP typically results in ORIGIN i. If a route is redistributed from OSPF into BGP without being originally created in BGP, it may show ORIGIN?. When comparing two otherwise equal paths, BGP prefers the lower ORIGIN type, with IGP best, then EGP, then Incomplete. A common misconception is treating ORIGIN as a long-term trust signal; it's only a simple indicator of how the route was introduced and is evaluated after AS_PATH in the selection process. Key takeaway: ORIGIN provides a simple ordering preference and helps you spot redistributed routes.

MED, or Multi-Exit Discriminator, is an attribute exchanged between eBGP peers to influence how an adjacent autonomous system selects among multiple entry points into your AS. A lower MED value is preferred. Think of MED as a polite hint to neighbors: if you have two connections into AS 65000 and you prefer inbound traffic to enter via one of them, advertise a lower MED on routes at that connection. For example, set MED 10 on routes received at the preferred entry and MED 100 on the other. Important nuances: MED is only a suggestion to the adjacent AS and many operators ignore it in favor of LOCAL_PREF or policy. MED defaults to 0 if not set. Also MED is often non-transitive, so it may not be forwarded unchanged across multiple ASes. A common mistake is relying on MED to change outbound routing for your own AS; it won't. Use MED for influencing an adjacent AS's inbound decisions, and pair it with clear peering agreements and testing. Always verify how the peer treats MED in your interconnection and avoid assuming universal compliance.

NEXT_HOP identifies the IP address of the router that should be used to reach an advertised prefix. For eBGP the next-hop is typically the directly connected neighbor; for iBGP the next-hop learned from an eBGP peer is often carried unchanged. That means your iBGP peers must have IGP reachability to that NEXT_HOP, otherwise the route will be unusable even if it looks attractive in BGP attributes. A classic example: Router R2 advertises 2.2.2.0/24 to R1 over eBGP and sets NEXT_HOP 192.0.2.2. R1 learns the route via iBGP and retains NEXT_HOP 192.0.2.2; if other iBGP routers do not have an IGP path to 192.0.2.2 they cannot install the route. A common mistake is assuming BGP alone provides forwarding reachability — BGP selects based on attributes but IGP must supply next-hop reachability. To mitigate this, networks often use next-hop-self on eBGP sessions to set the next-hop to the advertising router, or ensure the IGP advertises reachability to external next-hops. Key takeaway: NEXT_HOP is essential for forwarding and its reachability is evaluated as part of the best path algorithm. When a BGP router has multiple paths to the same prefix, it evaluates attributes in a strict order. The first four steps determine many real-world outcomes. Step 1 prefers the highest WEIGHT — a Cisco-only, local attribute that immediately wins when different. Step 2 prefers the highest LOCAL_PREF, an AS-wide setting that overrides AS_PATH and MED decisions when set differently. If WEIGHT and LOCAL_PREF tie, Step 3 prefers paths locally originated by the router, such as those installed with the network command or via redistribution. Step 4 prefers the shortest AS_PATH, so fewer AS hops are generally better. Concrete example: suppose two routes arrive — one learned from ISP-A with LOCAL_PREF 100 and AS_PATH length 2, and another learned from ISP-B with LOCAL_PREF 200 but longer AS_PATH. At step 2 the route with LOCAL_PREF 200 wins and the algorithm stops; AS_PATH is not even considered. A common misconception is thinking AS_PATH always decides the winner — LOCAL_PREF and WEIGHT are checked earlier. Closing question: given a tie in WEIGHT and LOCAL_PREF, did you check if any route is locally originated before comparing AS_PATH? That step often resolves ties in operational networks.

Continuing the best path sequence, Step 5 prefers the lowest ORIGIN type (IGP over EGP over Incomplete). If ORIGIN ties, Step 6 prefers the lowest MED, which influences inbound selection by adjacent ASes. Step 7 prefers eBGP paths over iBGP paths when all previous attributes are equal — this usually favors paths learned from external peers. Step 8 prefers the path with the lowest IGP cost to the BGP NEXT_HOP; this is a practical step because the selected BGP path must be reachable for forwarding. For example, if two paths have the same WEIGHT, LOCAL_PREF, origin and MED, but one path's NEXT_HOP is reachable with IGP cost 10 and the other has cost 5, the algorithm will select the lower IGP cost path. A frequent operational oversight is not checking IGP reachability: a route with great BGP attributes but an unreachable NEXT_HOP will not be used. Another misconception is assuming MED applies globally; MED is an inter-AS hint often ignored by peers. Key takeaway: beyond the early attribute checks, reachability considerations and eBGP preference play a crucial role in final selection.

When all previous attributes are equal, BGP uses final tie-breakers to ensure deterministic selection. Step 9 prefers the oldest path to reduce route-flap churn when comparing multiple paths from the same eBGP peer. Step 10 prefers the path from the BGP router with the lowest Router ID as a tie-breaker. If a tie still remains, Step 11 prefers the path from the neighbor with the lowest IP address. These last checks are operational safeguards to avoid non-deterministic behavior and ensure stable forwarding without oscillation. Concrete example: if two sessions from the same AS present identical attributes, the route learned earlier will be preferred; if they were learned simultaneously, the lower Router ID or neighbor IP will decide. A misconception is thinking these are policy knobs — they are not intended for traffic engineering, but as deterministic fallbacks. Key takeaway: the algorithm always results in one chosen path. If you need to change selection earlier, adjust WEIGHT or LOCAL_PREF; relying on final tie-breakers is brittle and unlikely to survive topology changes. Let's summarize the essentials you should keep in mind. First, attributes carry the policy and context that BGP uses to pick a single best route; they are grouped by propagation rules and recognition. Second, scope matters: WEIGHT is local to a router, LOCAL_PREF is AS-wide, AS_PATH and ORIGIN are transitive and visible across AS boundaries, MED is a hint to adjacent ASes, and NEXT_HOP must be reachable via IGP for forwarding. Third, the best path algorithm evaluates attributes in a strict order — WEIGHT, LOCAL_PREF, local origination, AS_PATH, ORIGIN, MED, eBGP over iBGP, IGP cost to NEXT_HOP, and final tie-breakers like age and Router ID. Finally, always validate changes in a lab environment and check both BGP and IP routing tables after modifying attributes. These points will help you design predictable traffic-engineering policies and avoid common pitfalls like assuming WEIGHT propagates or expecting MED to always be honored.

Use these three quick reminders when you work in the lab or on production networks. First, always consider attribute scope before you change it: WEIGHT affects only the local router, LOCAL_PREF is AS-wide, and MED is an inter-AS hint. Second, understand the selection order: early attributes like WEIGHT and LOCAL_PREF trump AS_PATH or MED, so change the earliest attribute necessary to get the intended behavior. Third, verify both BGP and IGP: NEXT_HOP reachability is required for forwarding and IGP cost can decide the best path when BGP attributes tie. These short checks will reduce configuration errors and make your traffic-engineering predictable and safe.
